articles.title: This CO2-powered cooling jacket could keep you comfortable in extreme heat without a battery - Yanko Design

articles.full_text:
Most wearable cooling devices add more hardware to what you are already wearing. Hissy, developed by five designers as part of Samsung Design Membership, is different though. the concept puts a CO₂-powered cooling system inside a lightweight technical jacket, turning the garment itself into an air-delivery system.
The idea comes from a fairly simple problem. Portable fans can struggle when the surrounding air is already extremely hot, while battery-powered cooling systems bring their own compromises in weight, runtime, and heat management. Hissy replaces the usual fan-and-battery setup with a small CO₂ cartridge mounted at the wrist. When the cartridge is connected, high-pressure liquid carbon dioxide vaporizes inside the cooling hardware, producing airflow at around -30 Degree Celsius.
What makes the jacket interesting, however, is what happens after the cold air is generated. Rather than dumping it into the garment and hoping it reaches the right places, Hissy routes it through a tubular Air Path built into the jacket. The path follows a spiral around the body, and the jacket is cut and stitched around this structure. Its shape also helps prevent the tube from sharply bending or kinking as the wearer moves.
Small perforations along the Air Path release the cold air at selected points. The designers determined their positioning and size using thermal mapping and heat-distribution tests, concentrating the airflow around areas where the body produces more heat. That explains the unusual construction of the jacket. The visible pattern isn’t simply there for visual effect; it traces the route the cooling system needs to take through the garment.
The CO₂ cartridge itself sits in a surprisingly neat docking system. Instead of being screwed into place, it attaches magnetically. Locking protrusions keep it from being pulled straight out while the system is operating, and rotating the cartridge changes the magnetic interaction so it can be released. An internal strap and sleeve zipper keep the hardware secure around the wrist, while a chest pocket provides somewhere to carry additional cartridges.
There is also an effort to make the disposable-looking cartridge system less wasteful. Hissy proposes using CO₂ captured from industrial processes as the cooling medium. Once a cartridge is empty, it can be collected, inspected, refilled, and returned to circulation. The designers see this as a way of keeping both the cartridge and the captured gas within a reuse cycle rather than treating them as single-use components.
For now, Hissy is a design concept rather than a product you can buy, but the team isn’t limiting the idea to jackets. Its proposed roadmap includes applying the same cooling technology to footwear, followed by products such as outdoor can coolers. A later version could even become a thermal-management system for machines working outdoors in high temperatures, including delivery robots and drones.
I couldn’t stop thinking “Una-Mug” when I first saw this project. That’s not the name at all! It’s called “Umarmung,” and it’s basically a floor-level-chair….
Wearing sunglasses serves many purposes. Others may just be getting stylish pairs for fashion fix but there are more people who wear them for protection….
To quote Don Norman, “Everything has a personality: everything sends an emotional signal. Even where this was not the intention of the designer, the people…

According to the affidavit the FSSAI presented to the Supreme Court, the proposal is to roll out the labelling in two phases. The first will apply to products that exceed the standard limits in two of the three additives and the second phase will extend the labelling to products that exceed the limits in at least one of the three. It is unclear when the new policy will begin and how long it will take for the transition. This is important since the first phase could offer considerable leeway for companies. A packaged product that has a high sugar content but not high levels of salt or fat — such as a standard cold drink — could escape the red hexagon, although its consumption is now acknowledged as harmful. Second, the FSSAI guidelines refer to added sugar and added saturated fat, which can offer an escape route to scores of “health foods” and breakfast cereals that have high sugar and saturated fat content embedded in the ingredients themselves.
Packaged fruit juices that purport to have no added sugar would, for instance, escape the red hexagon. But this, too, could be somewhat misleading. The juicing process in itself tends to concentrate natural sugars by removing the fibre, which causes sugar spikes. That could be harmful for borderline diabetics. Although most of the domestic demand for packaged foods in India is met from local producers, imported packaged foods are also appearing on Indian dining-tables in larger quantities. These, too, should be subject to similar labelling. Given the vibrant variety of local snacks that Indians consume — from laddoos to samosas, in which any or all these ingredients are lavishly used — the FSSAI would provide a signal service to the cause of public health by considering similar mandatory labelling in sweet shops and other establishments selling these products.
It is a moot point, however, whether enhanced labelling can actually deter consumption. For years, the statutory warning on cigarette packets did nothing to reduce smoking. Studies show that it was only after graphic pictorial warnings on packs were made mandatory that consumption dropped, with many smokers quitting, though in this case, steadily rising excise duty also played a part. Replicating this on food warnings will be difficult and perhaps avoidable. But the government has a wide array of public communication devices available to it to spread the word about healthy eating — television, radio, billboards, and digital media. A sustained long-term campaign to accompany the red hexagon rollout would go a long way towards educating an increasingly obese and unhealthy middle class of the virtues of healthy eating.
